title: The poem and its occasion
short: A blank-verse monologue in Men and Women (1855), subtitled 'Called "The Faultless Painter"', spoken by the Florentine painter Andrea del Sarto (1486-1530) to his wife.
body: Browning drew on Vasari's Life of Andrea (Vasari had been Andrea's pupil), which praises his technically flawless work but blames his wife and his timid nature for his failure to equal Raphael and Michelangelo. A story recorded by Mrs Andrew Crosse (1900) says John Kenyon asked the Brownings for a copy of the Pitti double portrait thought to show Andrea and his wife; unable to obtain a good copy, Browning sent the poem instead. Historians treat the tale cautiously, and the portrait's identification is itself doubtful. The poem opens in the middle of a conversation, after a quarrel, a typical monologue device.

title: Blank verse and the silent listener
short: Unrhymed iambic pentameter addressed to a listener who never speaks; her responses are inferred from Andrea's words.
body: Unlike the rhymed, enjambed couplets of 'My Last Duchess', this monologue uses a slow, conversational blank verse, full of pauses, dashes and broken sentences, matching Andrea's weariness. Lucrezia's reactions (turning her face, smiling, listening for the Cousin's whistle) are registered only through his words, a technique that lets the reader see what Andrea half-refuses to acknowledge. Langbaum's theory of the monologue, balancing sympathy and judgment, has often been illustrated from this poem, where Andrea's self-excuses are both moving and evasive.

title: Lucrezia
short: Lucrezia del Fede, a widow whom Andrea married; Vasari portrays her as vain and unfaithful and as the model for his Madonnas.
body: Vasari, who disliked her, describes Lucrezia as a beautiful but proud and jealous woman who dominated Andrea and alienated his friends and pupils. Browning adopts this view but complicates it: Andrea's own weakness, not merely his wife, is exposed. The poem assumes she is meeting a lover, the 'Cousin', and that her 'friend's friend' commissions pictures as part of that arrangement. Several critics also hear in Andrea's dependence on an uncomprehending wife a deliberate inversion of the Brownings' own marriage of two poets.

title: Fiesole
short: An ancient hill town just north-east of Florence, visible from the city; its 'sober pleasant' look at evening matches Andrea's toned-down art.
body: Fiesole, the Etruscan and Roman Faesulae, stands on a hill overlooking Florence. In the poem the view becomes an emblem of Andrea's temperament and art: 'My youth, my hope, my art, being all toned down / To yonder sober pleasant Fiesole' (ll. 39-40). The convent wall, the bell and the 'last monk' leaving the garden (ll. 41-44) complete a scene of dusk and enclosure.

title: my everybody's moon
short: Lucrezia is like the moon: beautiful, cold, looked at by everyone and seeming to belong to each, yet looking at no one.
body: The image works on several levels. The moon reflects borrowed light and shines indifferently on all; Lucrezia's beauty is public, and Andrea suspects she is 'looked on by' other men in turn. The moon is also traditionally changeable and associated with inconstancy. Andrea's tone wavers between tenderness and bitter insight, ending lamely, 'very dear, no less'. The passage illustrates how the monologue reveals Andrea's knowledge of her infidelity, which he will not openly confront.

title: A common grayness
short: The evening light gives a uniform silver-grey tone to the scene, an image of Andrea's even, subdued painting and of his diminished life.
body: 'Harmony' is the painter's term for the balanced relation of tones and colours. Andrea's own work was admired for its soft, blended tonality and delicate modelling. The 'grayness' recurs as a leitmotif ('All is silver-gray / Placid and perfect with my art', ll. 98-99; 'the gray remainder of the evening', l. 227), set against the 'golden' days in France (l. 168). Grey suggests technical refinement but also emotional twilight, lack of passion and resignation.

title: autumn in everything
short: The season of decline mirrors Andrea's sense that his life and art have passed their prime.
body: The details of the scene, the clinking chapel bell, the convent wall holding the trees, the last monk leaving the garden, 'days decrease', build a mood of ending. Browning gives Andrea a painter's sense of composition: the scene 'seems to fall into a shape' (l. 46). The passage is an example of the monologue's use of setting to externalise the speaker's state of mind; the time of day and year match his weariness ('I am grown peaceful as old age to-night', l. 244), though historically Andrea was under forty.

title: A twilight-piece
short: A painting of an evening scene; Andrea sees his own life composed like such a picture, harmonious but dim.
body: Andrea views 'my work and self / And all that I was born to be and do' as a single composition. Immediately he turns to fatalism: 'Love, we are in God's hand' and 'So free we seem, so fettered fast we are!' (ll. 49-51). Critics note that his invocations of God and fate tend to excuse his lack of will; he accepts the 'fetter' rather than resisting. The self-pictorialising also shows his habit of turning experience into aesthetic surface.

title: cartoon
short: A full-scale preparatory drawing on stout paper, used to transfer a design to a wall or panel.
body: In Renaissance workshops a 'cartoon' (Italian cartone, from carta, paper) was a full-size drawing whose outlines were pricked or traced onto the plaster or panel (OED). The modern sense of a humorous drawing dates from the 1840s. Andrea points with pride to a Madonna design, and boasts that he can do 'with my pencil' (brush or drawing instrument) whatever he conceives, 'easily' and 'perfectly'. The boast is the poem's ironic premise: technical mastery without the striving of greater spirits.

title: less is more
short: Others with less skill achieve more spiritually; Andrea concedes that his technical superiority yields less.
body: Someone (unnamed: 'I know his name, no matter') says the struggling painters 'do much less' than Andrea; Andrea turns this round: 'less is more', their imperfect works are worth more because they express a 'truer light of God'. The phrase was later made famous as a motto of modernist architecture (Mies van der Rohe), with a very different meaning (simplicity as virtue). Here it expresses Browning's recurrent doctrine of the value of imperfection, which the poem states at l. 97. 'I am judged' means both 'I am condemned' and 'my case is decided'.

title: Morello
short: Monte Morello, the mountain to the north-west of Florence, seen in the background of Andrea's painting and from his window.
body: Monte Morello is the highest hill close to Florence. Andrea imagines a critic objecting that the mountain's outline in a painting is 'wrongly traced', and asks 'what does the mountain care?' (l. 96): the real mountain is indifferent to praise or blame, as Andrea claims to be. At dusk Morello disappears from view ('Morello's gone', l. 209), marking the progress of the evening across the monologue.

title: reach and grasp
short: The poem's most famous lines: aspiration should exceed achievement, otherwise heaven, the goal beyond reach, would have no meaning.
body: The lines state a central Browningesque idea, the 'glory of the imperfect': human worth lies in striving beyond what can be attained, and the gap between aspiration and achievement implies a fulfilment beyond this life. Ironically it is Andrea, who reaches only what he can grasp, who utters it; the maxim condemns him. The rest of the line, 'All is silver-gray / Placid and perfect with my art: the worse!', applies it at once. Compare Browning's 'A Grammarian's Funeral' and 'Rabbi Ben Ezra' ('What I aspired to be, / And was not, comforts me').

title: The Urbinate
short: Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio, 1483-1520), born at Urbino; his death 'five years ago' sets the monologue in 1525.
body: Raphael died in Rome in April 1520, so the dramatic date is about 1525. The painting is a copy sent by 'George Vasari', the art historian Giorgio Vasari (1511-74), who studied with Andrea and later wrote the Lives on which the poem draws; the anglicised 'George' is Browning's touch. Andrea, a superb draughtsman, can see that an arm in Raphael's picture is 'wrongly put', yet recognises that its 'soul is right' (ll. 111-113). Raphael (spelled 'Rafael') thus stands for inspired imperfection against Andrea's faultlessness.

title: the fowler's pipe
short: Lucrezia's voice lures Andrea as a bird-catcher's whistle lures a bird into the net.
body: A fowler is a hunter of wild birds, who used a pipe or call to imitate birdsong and draw birds into a snare (OED). The image recalls the biblical 'snare of the fowler' (Psalm 91:3, 124:7). Andrea's soul 'hears' her voice and 'follows to the snare': he presents himself as the willing victim of her beauty, though the poem invites us to see the passivity as his own.

title: Agnolo
short: Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475-1564), 'Michel Agnolo' in the Tuscan form; with Raphael and Leonardo, the standard of greatness Andrea measures himself against.
body: Browning uses the Tuscan form Agnolo for Angelo. Andrea imagines Lucrezia urging him on 'side by side with Agnolo' and 'up to God, all three'. Later (ll. 183-193) he recalls Michelangelo telling Raphael that a 'sorry little scrub' in Florence (Andrea) would make him sweat if given equal commissions. I have not found that compliment in Vasari's Life of Andrea, and its source is uncertain; Browning may have shaped it from Florentine tradition. Andrea values it above everything, yet cannot act on it.

title: All is as God overrules
short: Andrea retreats into providence and fatalism, a pattern of self-excuse that runs through the poem.
body: Having imagined that a more ambitious wife might have spurred him to greatness, Andrea immediately retracts: 'Perhaps not', 'incentives come from the soul's self', and finally 'God, I conclude, compensates, punishes'. The aphorism 'In this world, who can do a thing, will not; / And who would do it, cannot' (ll. 137-138) defines the 'half-men' who have either will or power but not both. Critics such as Roma King see Andrea's oscillation between self-assertion and acknowledged weakness as the poem's psychological core.

title: Francis I and Fontainebleau
short: Francis I of France invited Andrea to his court in 1518; Andrea's 'kingly days' there are the poem's golden memory.
body: According to Vasari, Andrea went to France at the invitation of Francis I (reigned 1515-47), the great patron who also brought Leonardo to France. He was honoured and well paid, but returned to Florence at Lucrezia's urging, with money the king had entrusted to him to buy works of art, which he spent instead on a house. Fontainebleau was the king's palace south-east of Paris. Browning's lines on the king's 'golden look', the 'jingle of his gold chain' and 'such frank French eyes' give the memory a radiance that contrasts with the 'gray' present.

anchor: the other's Virgin was his wife
title: the other's Virgin was his wife
short: Andrea imagines posterity excusing him because he used his wife as model for his Madonnas, a detail drawn from Vasari.
body: Vasari records that Andrea rarely painted a woman's face without using Lucrezia as model. Andrea pictures future viewers saying that Raphael's picture is better 'when you pray', but that Andrea had the consolation of a beautiful wife. The irony is that the wife he idealises as the Virgin is unfaithful. 'The Roman' is Raphael, who worked chiefly in Rome. Andrea's longing to paint 'the Virgin's face' again, 'Not yours this time!' (ll. 230-231), hints at a wish to escape her.

title: scrub
short: A mean, insignificant fellow; Michelangelo's affectionate disparagement is the highest praise Andrea has received.
body: 'Scrub' in this sense means an undersized or contemptible person (OED). The speech attributed to Michelangelo says that this obscure Florentine, if 'pricked on' by popes and kings as Raphael is, would 'bring the sweat into that brow of yours'. Andrea then corrects Raphael's drawing in chalk, only to stop himself: 'Ay, but the soul! he's Rafael! rub it out!' (l. 197). The gesture enacts the poem's argument in miniature.

anchor: And indeed the arm is wrong
title: the arm is wrong
short: Andrea can correct Raphael's anatomy, but recognises that correctness is not the same as genius.
body: The flaw in Raphael's drawing, first noticed at l. 111, returns. Andrea briefly asserts his superiority and calls for chalk, then erases his correction. Browning dramatises the distinction, central to Victorian art criticism (notably Ruskin), between technical finish and imaginative or spiritual expression. Andrea's competence is real; what he lacks is the 'play, the insight and the stretch' (l. 116).

title: cue-owls
short: Scops owls, called chiù in Italian from their call; they 'speak the name we call them by' because the name imitates their cry.
body: The scops owl, a small Mediterranean owl, has a clear, repeated call rendered 'kew' or 'chiù', from which its Italian name derives. Wright's English Dialect Dictionary records 'cue-owl' as an English rendering; the Scottish National Dictionary treats the word as an imitative coinage and suggests other owls, so the species is not certain. The detail marks nightfall ('settled dusk', l. 208) and gives the monologue its precise sense of time passing.

title: gold ... cement
short: Andrea imagines the walls of his house glowing with the king's misappropriated gold, a visionary image of guilt.
body: Vasari reports that Andrea spent money Francis I had given him to buy pictures on building himself a house in Florence. Here the walls, when Andrea's eyes are tired, seem lit up, the mortar replaced by 'fierce bright gold'. The image fuses guilt with the golden radiance of his French period. It anticipates the house as 'the melancholy little house / We built to be so gay with' (ll. 212-213) and the frank confession 'I took his coin, was tempted and complied' (l. 248).

title: The Cousin
short: Lucrezia's lover, euphemistically 'Cousin', whose gaming debts Andrea will pay with commissions; Andrea's complaisance is the poem's bleakest revelation.
body: The 'Cousin', whose whistle summons Lucrezia, is clearly her lover. Andrea knows of the 'loans' and 'gaming debts' and offers to pay them by taking on more commissions ('let smiles buy me!'). The 'friend' of l. 5 and l. 234 may be the same person or a patron connected to him. The 'thirteen scudi for the ruff' (l. 241) is the price of a pleated collar; scudi (Italian scudo, 'shield') were coins. The poem ends on 'Again the Cousin's whistle! Go, my Love', a final surrender.

title: The New Jerusalem
short: Andrea imagines a heavenly contest: the four walls of the holy city, measured by the angel's reed, to be painted by Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo and himself.
body: In Revelation 21 the heavenly city, the New Jerusalem, lies 'foursquare', and an angel measures it with 'a golden reed' (21:15-16). Andrea fancies each great painter covering one wall, and himself with an advantage, since the other three are 'without a wife' while he has his. The final irony is double: he still thinks Lucrezia an asset, and his imagined heavenly 'chance' is only another competition he will lose to them. 'Leonard' is Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519). 'Meted' means measured.

anchor: I do what many dream of
title: 'The faultless painter'
short: Andrea was known as 'senza errori', without errors; the poem's subtitle turns this praise into the measure of his failure.
body: Vasari's Life presents Andrea as a painter of almost flawless technique whose timid spirit kept him from the grandeur of his rivals; the epithet 'senza errori' summarises his reputation. Browning's subtitle, 'Called "The Faultless Painter"', is ironic: the poem argues that perfect execution without aspiration falls short of the flawed but soaring work of others whose 'works drop groundward' while 'themselves' reach 'a heaven that's shut to me' (ll. 83-84). Critics such as Hawlin connect this to Andrea's emotional and sexual timidity.
